optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.375em;"><strong>In this episode</strong></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>David Heinemeier Hansson (DHH) is the creator of Ruby on Rails and Omarchy, co-founder and CTO of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3f2bc402-a911-4623-bad2-332022050dc9?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">37signals</a><span> (maker of Basecamp and HEY), and the author of several books including the best-seller, </span><em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ab6e8e2a-a553-4c0f-82e0-2e2b681d4ae5?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Remote: Office Not Required</a></em><span>, co-written with </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c63b93fd-25e5-464a-8bd2-77327febf173?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Jason Fried</a><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Six months ago, in an episode of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/17505c2f-9929-4e1b-a4c2-0d5b334ab453?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">the Lex Fridman podcast</a><span>, David shared how he doesn’t use AI tools to write code: he types out all his code. But things have changed a lot since then.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In this episode, we discuss his approach to building software, how it’s changed in the last six months, and why he now takes an agent-first approach, and how he barely writes any code by hand. We go into how he uses AI agents: which alter how he builds and explores ideas, but also how his standards of quality and craft remain the same.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">We also discuss how 37signals thinks about product development, from the role of designers to the importance of aesthetics and taste. David gets into how he sees beauty and functionality as closely linked, and why strong opinions about design lead to better software.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Finally, we look into the uneven impact of AI which amplifies senior engineers while creating challenges for junior developers, and what this may mean for the role of the software engineer.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.375em;"><strong>Key observations from DHH</strong></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Here are 12 of my most interesting takeaways from talking with DHH:</p><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/de137879-1e21-4f90-88ad-4263a32aa481?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/JiWgKRgdgpI" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>1. His philosophy on AI has not changed, but the available tools very much have. </strong><span>Autocomplete-style coding assistants were genuinely annoying for experienced developers six months ago. Things changed with the shift from tab-completion to agent harnesses, plus the emergence of powerful models like Opus 4.5 – when agents started producing code which DHH does want to merge with little to no alteration.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>2. Beautiful code and products aren’t matters of vanity; they’re signals of correctness.</strong><span> Dipping into philosophy, DHH says: “When something is beautiful, it’s likely to be correct.” He argues that Steve Jobs wanted the </span><em>inside</em><span> of a computer to be beautiful because people who care about circuit board layout are also those who sweat on the details of the UI.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>3. DHH’s development workflow, today:</strong><span> he runs </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a4e7a941-c1ef-4d0f-8d23-e594ed4fd214?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">tmux</a><span> to have two models running, and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/424047ec-e91e-4380-8b64-eb73d40f5c57?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">neovim</a><span> in the center. Specifics:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">One fast LLM running (typically Gemini 2.5) in one split terminal</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">A slow but more powerful model in another terminal (usually Opus)</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>NeoVim for reviewing diffs via </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c9041b51-2b67-4ea3-bd2e-3ee6f5afa95c?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Lazygit</a></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>4. Ruby on Rails seems to be enjoying a Renaissance thanks to AI.</strong><span> Rails is one of the most token-efficient ways of building web apps and is well-suited for agent workflows. Testing is part of the framework, which helps agents write tests and validate their own outputs. It also produces code that humans can read and verify, which matters when reviewing agent output at speed.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>5. A big win from using AI agents is tackling stuff that you wouldn’t have before.</strong><span> A senior engineer at 37signals ran a “P1 optimization” project to improve the </span><em>fastest</em><span> 1% of requests. They optimized the P1 from being at 4 milliseconds, to under half a millisecond. This is the sort of work that wouldn’t have been considered previously!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>6. Running several AI agents feels less like “project management” and more like “wearing a mech suit.” </strong><span>Being a project manager of agents did not appeal to DHH, but now that he’s building with several agents, he feels like he’s in control of the work which is being hyper-accelerated.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>7. Senior engineers benefit from AI a lot more than juniors.</strong><span> At 37signals, senior engineers gain more from AI tools as they can validate whether an agent’s output is production-ready. DHH also notes that Amazon reached the same conclusion, and no longer lets junior programmers ship agent-generated code to production without review.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>8. 37signals has one designer for every two engineers.</strong><span> The company has around 20 software engineers and 10 designers. Designers do far more than design; they’re also product managers and “implementers” rolled into one. On top of making things look good, they figure out what should be built, how it should work, and often build the first version. DHH compares design at 37signals to jewelry design: “you should know the properties of gold. You should know how it bends.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>9. AI agents could turn 37signals’ “designer model” into the industry standard. </strong><span>AI tools now empower designers to implement more of their vision directly, and DHH suspects the rest of the industry is converging toward what 37signals has always done: working with small teams, where designers are also builders.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>10. Command Line Interfaces (CLI) feel like the ultimate AI interface, which validates the Unix philosophy of the 1970s</strong><span>. DHH is building CLIs for all 37signals products because they let agents chain tools together. “GitHub also has a CLI, and Sentry as well,” he says. “You can tie all these things together so an agent can check errors, write a fix, post a PR, and report back to basecamp.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>11. The demise of the two-month product development cycle described in the book </strong><em><strong>‘Shape Up: Stop Running in Circles and Ship Work that Matters’. </strong></em><span>The </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4994f4e7-4541-47ea-ace7-5a12286404ed?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">2019 title</a><span> by Ryan Signer covered how 37signals worked at the time, and DHH reveals that this methodology now needs rewriting because AI acceleration has made that timeline feel slow.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>12. Eight hours of sleep is non-negotiable – even during an AI gold rush!</strong><span> DHH believes the dopamine loop of shipping with agents is intoxicating and can lead to higher risk of burnout. So, he sleeps eight hours and doesn’t use an alarm.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro That's the ceiling on what you can build.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/700d4e08-7685-4767-b7f2-c5335b405f44?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: #7756e3;text-decoration: none;">WorkOS Pipes removes it.</a><span> One API call connects your product to the apps your users live in. Pull context from their tools, cross-reference data across silos, power AI agents that act across services. All with fresh, managed credentials you never have to think about.</span></p><p class="button-wrapper" data-attrs="{"url":"https://go.bytebytego.com/WorkOS_040826CTA","text":"Turn data to insight →","action":null,"class":null}" data-component-name="ButtonCreateButton" style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: center;cursor: pointer;border-radius: 4px;"><a class="button primary" href="https://substack.com/redirect/e4bfc2b6-9518-4f68-8785-a5b1531ea389?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="font-family: system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';display: inline-block;box-sizing: border-box;cursor: pointer;border: none;border-radius: 8px;font-size: 14px;line-height: 20px;font-weight: 600;text-align: center;margin: 0;opacity: 1;outline: none;white-space: nowrap;color: #ffffff !important;text-decoration: none !important;background-color: #7756e3;padding: 12px 20px;height: auto;"><span style="color: #ffffff;text-decoration: none;">Turn data to insight →</span></a></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Every Friday morning, a team at Spotify takes hundreds of code changes written by dozens of engineering teams and begins packaging them into a single app update. That update will eventually reach more than 675 million users on Android, iOS, and Desktop. They do this every single week. And somehow, more than 95% of those releases ship to every user without a hitch.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The natural assumption is that they’re either incredibly careful and therefore slow, or incredibly fast and therefore reckless. The truth is neither.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">How do you ship to 675 million users every week, with hundreds of changes from dozens of teams running on thousands of device configurations, without breaking things?</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The answer is not to test really hard. Spotify built a release architecture where speed and safety reinforce each other. In this article, we will take a look at this process in detail and attempt to derive learnings.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><em>Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from the Spotify Engineering Team. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.</em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;text-align: justify">The Two-Week Journey of a Spotify Release</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">To see how this works, let us follow a single release from code merge to production.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Spotify practices trunk-based development, which means that all developers merge their code into a single main branch as soon as it’s tested and reviewed. There are no long-lived feature branches where code sits in isolation for weeks. Everyone pushes to the same branch continuously, which keeps integration problems small but requires discipline and solid automated testing.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">See the diagram below that shows the concept of trunk-based development:</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" release cycle starts on a Friday morning. The version number gets bumped on the main branch. From that point, nightly builds start going out to Spotify employees and a group of external alpha testers. During this first week, teams develop and merge new code freely. Bug reports flow in from internal and alpha users. Crash rates and other quality metrics are tracked for each build, both automatically and by human review. When a crash or issue crosses a predefined severity threshold, a bug ticket gets created automatically. When something looks suspicious but falls below that threshold, the Release Manager can create one manually.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: Engineering Blog</a></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">On the Friday of the second week, the release branch gets cut, meaning a separate copy of the codebase is created specifically for this release. This is the key moment in the release cycle. From this point, only critical bug fixes are allowed on the release branch. Meanwhile, the main branch keeps moving. New features and non-critical fixes continue to merge there, destined for next week’s release. This separation is the mechanism that lets Spotify develop at full speed while simultaneously stabilizing what’s about to ship.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Teams then perform regression testing, checking that existing features still work correctly after the new changes, and report their results. Teams with high confidence in their automated tests and pre-merge routines can opt out of manual testing entirely. Beta testers receive builds from the more stable release branch, providing additional real-world runtime over the weekend.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">By Monday, the goal is to submit the app to the stores. By Tuesday, if the app store review passes and quality metrics look good, Spotify rolls it out to 1% of users. By Wednesday, if nothing alarming surfaces, they roll out to 100%.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The flow below shows all the steps in a typical release process:</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table Engineering Blog</a></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">As an example, for version 8.9.2, which carried the Audiobooks feature launch in new markets, this timeline played out almost exactly as planned. What made that possible was everything happening behind the timeline.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;">Rings of Exposure: Catching Bugs Where They’re Cheapest to Fix</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The code doesn’t go from a developer’s laptop to 675 million users in one jump. It passes through concentric rings of users, and each ring exists to catch a specific category of failure.</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">The first ring is Spotify’s own employees. They run nightly builds from the main branch, using the app the way real users do. This catches obvious functional bugs early. Even a crash that only affects a small number of employees gets investigated, because a bug that appears minor internally could signal a much larger problem once it hits millions of devices.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">The second ring is external alpha testers. These users introduce more device diversity and real-world usage patterns that the internal team may not have anticipated. They’re running builds that are still being actively developed, so rough edges are expected, but the data they generate is invaluable.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">The third ring is beta testers, who receive builds from the release branch rather than the main branch. These builds are expected to be more stable. Beta users provide additional runtime over weekends and evenings, and their feedback either builds confidence that the release is solid or surfaces issues that slipped through the first two rings.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">The fourth ring is the 1% production rollout. Real users, real devices, real conditions. Spotify’s user base is large enough that even 1% provides statistically meaningful data. If a severe issue appears during this phase, the rollout is paused immediately, and the responsible team starts working on a fix.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">The fifth and final ring is the 100% rollout. Only after the 1% rollout looks clean does the release go out to everyone.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">For reference, the Audiobooks launch in version 8.9.2 shows how this system works at an even more granular level.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The Audiobooks feature didn’t just pass through these five rings of app release. It had its own layered rollout on top of that. The feature code had been sitting in the app for multiple releases already, hidden behind a backend feature flag. It was turned on for most employees first. The team watched for any crash, no matter how small, that might indicate trouble. Only after the app release itself reached a sufficient user base did the Audiobooks team begin gradually enabling the feature for real users in specific markets, using the same backend flag to control the percentage.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">See the diagram below that shows the concept of a feature flag:</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" separation between deploying code and activating a feature is a powerful pattern in the Spotify release process. It allows code to sit in the app, baking in production conditions invisibly, and get turned on later. If something goes wrong after activation, the feature can be turned off without shipping a new release. At Spotify’s scale, feature flags are a core safety mechanism, though managing hundreds of them across a large organization, each with per-market and per-user-percentage controls, is its own engineering challenge.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The Release Manager also made a deliberate coordination decision for 8.9.2. Since the Audiobooks feature was a high-stakes launch with marketing events already scheduled, another major feature that had been planned for the same release was rescheduled to the following week. Fewer variables in a single release means easier diagnosis if something goes wrong. That kind of judgment call is one of the things that separates release management from pure automation.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;text-align: justify">From Jira to a Release Command Center</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The multi-ring system generates a lot of data, such as Crash rates, bug tickets, sign-off statuses, build verification results, and app store review progress. Someone has to make sense of all of it, and this wasn’t an easy task.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Before the Release Manager Dashboard existed, everything lived in Jira. The Release Manager had to jump between tickets, check statuses across multiple views, and verify conditions manually, all while answering questions from teams on Slack. It was easy to miss a small detail, and a missed detail could mean extra work or a bug slipping through.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">So the Release team built a dedicated command center with clear goals:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">Optimize for the Release Manager’s workflow</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">Minimize context switching</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">No open blocking bug tickets</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: real-world usage of the build</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">When everything goes green, the release is ready to advance.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The dashboard got off to a rocky start, however. The first version was slow and expensive. Every page reload triggered queries to all 10 of the source systems it depended on, causing long load times and high costs. The Spotify engineering team noted that each reload cost about as much as a decent lunch in Stockholm. After switching to caching and pre-aggregating data every five minutes, load time dropped to eight seconds, and the cost became negligible.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;">The Robot: Automating the Predictable, Keeping Humans for the Ambiguous</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The dashboard gave the Release Manager the information to make fast decisions.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">However, by analyzing the time-series data the dashboard generated, the team noticed that a lot of the time in the release cycle wasn’t spent on hard decisions, but waiting.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The biggest time sinks were testing and fixing bugs (unavoidable), waiting for app store approval (outside Spotify’s control), and delays from manually advancing a release when a step was completed outside working hours. That last one alone could cost up to 12 hours. If the app store approved a build at 11 PM, the release just sat there until someone woke up and clicked “next.”</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Therefore, the team built what they called “the Robot.”</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">It’s a backend service that models the release process as a state machine, a set of defined stages with specific conditions that must be met before moving to the next one. The Robot tracks seven states. The five states on the normal path forward are release branched, final release candidate (the build that will actually ship), submitted for app store review, rolled out to 1%, and rolled out to 100%. Two additional states handle problems, which means either the rollout gets paused or the release gets cancelled entirely.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">See the diagram below:</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td href="https://substack.com/redirect/e904bb93-3e7e-4e68-b822-f9824bc7672b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="text-decoration: underline;">Spotify Engineering Blog</a></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The Robot continuously checks whether the conditions for advancing to the next state are met. If manual testing is signed off, no blocking bugs are open, and automated tests pass on the latest commit on the release branch, the Robot automatically submits the build for app store review without human intervention. If the app store approves the build at 3 AM, the Robot initiates the 1% rollout immediately instead of waiting for someone to show up at the office.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The result was an average reduction of about eight hours per release cycle.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">However, the Robot doesn’t make the hard calls. It doesn’t decide whether a crash affecting users in a specific region is severe enough to block a release. It doesn’t decide whether a bug in a new feature like Audiobooks, with marketing events already scheduled, should delay the entire release or just the feature rollout. It doesn’t negotiate with feature teams about timing. Those decisions require judgment, context, and sometimes difficult conversations. The Release Manager handles all of them.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">This split is deliberate. Predictable transitions that depend on rule-checks get automated. Ambiguous decisions that require coordination and judgment stay with humans.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;text-align: justify">Conclusion</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Spotify ships weekly to 675 million users through a strong release architecture. Layered exposure catches bugs where they’re cheapest to fix and centralized tooling turns scattered data into fast decisions. Automation handles the predictable so humans can focus on the ambiguous.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The key lesson here is that speed and safety aren’t opposites. At Spotify, each one enables the other. A weekly cadence means each release carries fewer changes. Fewer changes mean less risk per release. Less risk means shipping with confidence.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Since a cancelled release only costs one week, not a month or a quarter, teams are more willing to kill a bad release rather than push it through and hope for the best.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><strong>References:</strong></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;margin-bottom: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><span>The recent </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3cef1ab2-f774-45df-9584-c1444618c08d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Pragmatic Summit</a><span> saw two legends of software development share a stage in what was one of the most popular sessions at our debut live event in San Francisco. In front of a packed audience, Martin Fowler and Kent Beck tackled a range of highly-relevant topics, with me hosting proceedings.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Martin and Kent go back decades, and Martin jokes that his career is “mostly about writing down Kent Beck’s ideas.” They first collaborated in the 1990s, and each has published influential books – ‘</span><em>Extreme Programming Explained’ </em><span>and </span><em>‘Test-Driven Development’ </em><span>by Kent, and </span><em>‘Refactoring’ </em><span>and</span><em> ‘Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture’ </em><span>by Martin.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>At the Pragmatic Summit, they each shared a wealth of hard-earned learnings and decades-worth of perspective, along with a healthy dose of skepticism. Needless to say, the conversation did not disappoint, and this article summarizes what we discussed in their own words. You can also </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c9deab1e-9bb7-4e5b-a2c0-f8daf5bedb70?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">check out the full recording</a><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">We cover:</p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Technology shifts similar to AI. </strong><span>The arrival of the microprocessor, introduction of object-oriented languages, the Internet, and agile software development principles were all major changes – but one big difference was that it took time for these technologies to be adopted. Not so with AI.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Agile and AI similarities. </strong><span>With Agile, company incentives were often misaligned, “snake oil” vendors were everywhere, and a “mid pack” of developers who resisted the change saw their career prospects hit. These trends look likely to repeat with AI.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>What’s happening inside companies</strong><span>. There’s some confusion – and even panic – at large companies, while AI tools don’t work nearly as well on large and complex codebases as on greenfield projects. Also, a “re-soloing” of software development is inbound.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Avoiding burnout with AI agents</strong><span>. Set and maintain boundaries, and pay attention. Martin suggests to catch when you start producing “negative value”: that’s when to take a break.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Unhealthy performance metrics.</strong><span> Companies are starting to measure things like frequency of pull requests – when they should be looking to quantify outcomes and results.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Lower quality on purpose? </strong><span>It seems every business is optimizing for speed with AI, but quality can get dropped. Also: building features is more obvious with AI, than investing in “futures.”</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Test-Driven Development (TDD): tests no longer optional? </strong><span>Kent pioneered TDD, and today it’s more relevant than ever for working with AI.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Thriving in an AI-native industry.</strong><span> Focus on working with agents to express your craft, try to get more enjoyment in </span><em>understanding</em><span> your domain, and take on more ambitious work.</span></p></li></ol><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;">1. Technology shifts similar to AI</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Do you recall a tech change as similarly promising and unpredictable as AI?</strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Martin: </strong><span>“Nothing has hit with the magnitude of AI. This is a whole size different from anything we’ve faced before. On a smaller scale, we were very much involved in the growth of object oriented languages, which scared a lot of people. It didn’t scare us so much because we were part of it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Looking back, the internet had a huge impact on us all, and of course, Agile software development, too. Agile had a very big impact on a lot of organizations: you could tell by how hard they resisted it. We had to persuade people of the importance of these technological changes; yes, even the internet! It may sound surprising but there were people who didn’t think it was important.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The thing about AI is that today there is no argument about how important it is.”</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: of the microprocessor. Before that, computers were big boxes; you couldn’t move them around. If you wanted another computer, you’d mortgage your house for it. Having a computer was a </span><em>big</em><span> deal.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I was a kid in Silicon Valley with my dad as a programmer when the Intel 4004 hit the market [in 1971]. We went: “Wait a minute, that </span><em>chip</em><span> is a computer? Oh my goodness!” The possibilities of computing suddenly expanded thanks to it. If you could figure out how to write software on this chip and figure out how to design hardware around this thing, you could suddenly do things you hadn’t even imagined.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And so I think part of AI is this expansion of imagination. I’m writing projects that are ridiculously ambitious: I’m working on a persistent </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3e473c6b-7da8-46ce-a73e-dd0b648f152d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Smalltalk</a><span>. I’m writing library-quality code for Rust.”</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 Source: </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c06f6d77-80b7-42f4-b8d5-9f2a20e73a49?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="text-decoration: underline;">Intel</a></em></figcaption></figure></div><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.375em;">Balancing skepticism and curiosity</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>What was the feeling in the industry during those revolutions, and the differences between professionals who thrived back then and those who didn’t?</strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Martin:</strong><span> “There was a mix of people chasing the hype and those saying, “this new thing is nothing special.” I think you’ve always got to have that balance of skepticism and curiosity, and to be selective about it. I mean, I have been completely skeptical about some big changes: Blockchain was one I was extremely skeptical about.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">My skepticism is well-rooted because I’ve seen so much “snake oil” over the years. In fact, my skepticism has to be absolute and total, which means I have to be skeptical about my skepticism! To be that skeptical also requires curiosity: you’ve got to be curious enough to say “how do I probe in order to detect signs of something useful?”</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>You also need to be aware that your early interactions may not actually be a </span><em>true</em><span> signal. When I started playing around with AI, it was with GitHub Copilot a year and a half ago. I was pretty unimpressed; it would give you something wonderful, but most of the time it gave you such garbage that you would just delete it right away. If that had been my only impression of AI, I would’ve immediately flipped the “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d863b9fe-bab6-43d0-af3a-3d4821adb74f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">bozo bit</a><span>” on it, like I did with blockchain.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Kent:</strong><span> “Here’s the thing, the capabilities of AI can change week to week. I’ll try something with Gemini one week and it fails miserably. Then Claude Code works pretty well, and then it doesn’t. And then I try Gemini for the same thing and it works, when it hadn’t worked last week!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>People want an answer, but the answer’s always changing. In this environment, you can’t possibly have </span><em>the </em><span>answer. That’s the bad news, but the good news is that nobody else has the answer either. So, you’re just as smart as everybody else because we’re all equally ignorant.”</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;">2. Agile and AI similarities</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>In 2001, the ‘Agile Manifesto’ came out, of which you were both co-authors. I think many companies are expecting the same thing with AI as Agile promised: better, faster, cheaper software. But how did Agile adoption really play out?</strong></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;"><em>Full house: The conversation with Martin (left) and Kent (right) drew a large audience</em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Kent:</strong><span> “It turns out people don’t want faster, cheaper, better! Inside some companies, the incentives are misaligned with actually achieving that. And so as geeks trying to achieve these improvements and saying: “it’s 40% better, 12% cheaper and less fattening,” people will punish you if that doesn’t align with </span><em>their</em><span> incentives inside organizations.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In the ideal organization, everybody would care about the same things, but that’s just not the way it works! So, if AI is coming along to promise the same things, we’re going to see the same reaction as before.”</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Martin:</strong><span> “An obvious difference is the sheer magnitude and speed there is with AI. Also, I think there will be a big difference between people who use it well and people who use it badly. The trick is figuring out how to use it well and putting the effort in to learn. There will be a big distinction between those two groups.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But I suspect there will still be some similarities with Agile. The core notions behind Agile and extreme programming are solid and good, but a huge snake-oil industry appeared around it – the “Agile industrial complex”, as I refer to it. This is also happening with AI right now, and it’s often hard to see the difference between snake oil and the real stuff.”</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.375em;">AI as an amplifier</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Kent:</strong><span> “AI is an amplifier. If you’re young and learning quickly, AI can amplify your learning. I personally think this is the golden age of the junior programmer. I get people coming to me all the time saying things like “my son started his second year in CS and wants to go into something more commercial like art history.” And I’d say, “this is like if you’re a carpenter and they just introduced the circular saw and you think, ‘oh, well, carpentry is over. Anybody can build a house now.’ Well, no! Now, you have more powerful tools. You have less of the crummy work to do.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I think that young people are going to learn faster, and experienced folks who are working effectively are going to work quicker and more effectively.”</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.375em;">Developers stuck in the middle</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Kent: </strong><span>My concern is that there’s a “middle” of people who got into programming as a way to make money. If we look back at the Dotcom crash, there was a “mid pack” of such people who ended up going into real estate, more or less. But today, I don’t know where that “middle” will go, and it’s also much bigger now than 25 years ago.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Martin:</strong><span> “But that middle has also been “flushed out” to some degree by retrenchment in the software industry at the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/38b32e6a-7e8a-4b7a-b88d-c866c7049e26?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">end of the zero interest rate period</a><span>. So, that’s an interesting difference because we’ve had these things occurring at once: the AI boom, and the economic headwinds of the past 2-3 years.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is an interesting mix that wasn’t present in the ‘90s with the Dotcom Boom. Back then, it was pretty much </span><em>all</em><span> a solid boom.”</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.375em;">Return of “let’s get rid of programmers!”</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Kent: </strong><span>“Another interesting confluence of factors is the periodic, “we can get rid of all the programmers, woo-hoo” trend, which started with Cobol in the 1970s. With Cobol, business analysts were supposedly going to be able to write the programs, and the logic was that we wouldn’t need programmers anymore. That comes back repeatedly.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Agile, however, was definitely </span><em>not</em><span> a “let’s get rid of programmers” trend. With Agile, we wanted programmers to be more </span><em>effective</em><span> in their jobs. And since we started it, and were programmers, we were able to push that agenda pretty effectively.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">However, today the “get rid of programmers” trend is repeating. As programmers, it behooves us to think about why they keep wanting to get rid of us. Some of that’s about us as programmers, and some of it not. Still, we should think about why people periodically want to axe us. In the end, this trend amps up the fear factor that everybody’s experiencing.”</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.375em;">Return of “let’s get rid of programmers!”</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Kent: </strong><span>“Another interesting confluence of factors is the periodic, “we can get rid of all the programmers, woo-hoo” trend, which started with Cobol in the 1970s. 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.375em;">“Re-soloing” of programming</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Kent:</strong><span> “A big trend is the “re-soloing” [reduced in-person collaboration] of programming.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A big part of extreme programming (XP) was creating a safe social environment for basically antisocial people.</span><em> </em><span>On an XP team, people are talking to each other for hours a day, and are happy to do so because it’s set up to be a positive experience.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Now, I see programmers saying, “I’ve got six agents, so really I’m managing a team.” No, you’re not: you’re using six tools at once, which is fine, but it’s very different from having a conversation with somebody who sees things slightly differently, or has a different energy level from you on the day.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">We used to have programmers in individual offices with doors, and you’d shut the door and slide the pizza underneath. That was easy to manage, but then along came this messy, social, complicated, chaotic process of software development, which just happened to produce really good results.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But now, instead of 50 people on my team, I can have five and they don’t have to talk to each other, and each can have 10 agents. Is that the same? No, it’s not.”</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.375em;">More effective two-pizza teams & the future of pairing</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Martin: </strong><span>“Are we seeing two-pizza teams [of 5-10 people] becoming one-pizza teams because agents don’t eat pizza, or do we see two-pizza teams staying and becoming much more effective and capable? My bet is on more effective two-pizza teams.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">We’re beginning to see some interesting feedback in terms of pair programming. With pair programming, is it one human and the genie (AI) programming, or is it two humans and one genie? If it’s two of us, perhaps we can control the genie a bit better, and we also have interaction.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I’ll be very interested in reports of people trying to control genies in pairs, possibly even beyond pairs. There’s also the whole ‘mob programming’ thing, and how that will go with genies. I don’t necessarily think that one person and many genies is the right answer.”</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Kent</strong><span>: “My experience of pairing with two humans, plus one or more genies, has been very positive. And the fact the AI is slow is really nice. Every time models come out and are faster, I’m like, “Oh, there’s less time to talk.” When the AI goes away for three minutes, we can talk about our philosophy of naming, or how we express conditionals, or about what we should be doing next. But if it pops back in 15 seconds, you don’t have time for that conversation.”</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;">4. style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Nextdoor operates as a hyper-local social networking service that connects neighbors based on their geographic location.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The platform allows people to share local news, recommend local businesses, and organize neighborhood events. Since the platform relies on high-trust interactions within specific communities, the data must be both highly available and extremely accurate.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">However, as the service scaled to millions of users across thousands of global neighborhoods, the underlying database architecture had to evolve from a simple setup into a sophisticated distributed system.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">This engineering journey at Nextdoor highlights a fundamental rule of system design.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Every performance gain introduces a new requirement for data integrity. The team followed a predictable progression, moving from a single database instance to a complex hierarchy of connection poolers, read replicas, versioned caches, and background reconcilers. In this article, we will look at how the Nextdoor engineering team handled this evolution and the challenges they faced.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><em>Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from the Nextdoor Engineering Team. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.</em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;text-align: justify">The Limits of the “Big Box”</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">In the early days, Nextdoor relied on a single PostgreSQL instance to handle every post, comment, and neighborhood update.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">For many growing platforms, this is the most logical starting point. It is simple to manage, and PostgreSQL provides a robust engine capable of handling significant workloads. However, as more neighbors joined and the volume of simultaneous interactions grew, the team hit a wall that was not related to the total amount of data stored, but more to do with the connection limit.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">PostgreSQL uses a process-per-connection model. In other words, every time an application worker wants to talk to the database, the server creates a completely new process to handle that request. If an application has five thousand web workers trying to access the database at the same time, the server must manage five thousand separate processes. Each process consumes a dedicated slice of memory and CPU cycles just to exist.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Managing thousands of processes creates a massive overhead for the operating system. The server eventually spends more time switching between these processes than it does running the actual queries that power the neighborhood feed. This is often the point where vertical scaling, or buying a larger server with more cores, starts to show diminishing returns. The overhead of the “process-per-connection” model remains a bottleneck regardless of how much hardware is thrown at the problem.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">To solve this, Nextdoor introduced a layer of middleware called PgBouncer. This is a connection pooler that sits between the application and the database. Instead of every application worker maintaining its own dedicated line to the database, they all talk to PgBouncer.</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong>The Request Phase:</strong><span> A web worker requests a connection from PgBouncer to execute a quick query.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong>The Assignment Phase: </strong><span>PgBouncer assigns an idle connection from its pre-established pool rather than forcing the database to create a new process.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong>The Execution Phase:</strong><span> The query runs against the database using that shared connection.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong>The Release Phase:</strong><span> The worker finishes its task, and the connection returns to the pool immediately for the next worker to use.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">This allows thousands of application workers to share a few hundred “warm” database connections. This effectively removed the connection bottleneck and allowed the primary database to focus entirely on data processing.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;text-align: justify">Dividing the Labor and the “Lag” Problem</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Once connection management was stable, the next bottleneck appeared in the form of read traffic.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">In a social network like Nextdoor, the ratio of people reading the feed compared to people writing a post is heavily skewed. For every one person who saves a new neighborhood update, hundreds of others might view it. A single database server must handle both the “Writes” and the “Reads” at the same time. This creates resource contention where heavy read queries can slow down the ability of the system to save new data.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The solution was to move to a Primary-Replica architecture. In this setup, one database server is designated as the Primary. It is the only server allowed to modify or change data. Several other servers, known as Read Replicas, maintain copies of the data from the Primary. All the “Read” traffic from the application is routed to these replicas, while only the “Write” traffic goes to the Primary.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">See the diagram below:</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: However, this introduces the challenge of Asynchronous Replication. The Primary database sends its changes to the replicas using a stream of logs. It takes time for a new post saved on the Primary to travel across the network and appear on the replicas. This delay is known as replication lag.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">See the diagram below that shows the difference solve the issue of a neighbor making a post and then seeing it disappear upon a refresh, Nextdoor uses Time-Based Dynamic Routing. This is a smart routing logic that ensures users always see the results of their own actions. Here’s how it works:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong>The Write Marker:</strong><span> When a user performs a write action, like posting a comment, the application notes the exact timestamp of that event.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong>The Protected Window:</strong><span> For a specific period of time after that write, often a few seconds, the system treats that specific user as sensitive</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong>Dynamic Routing:</strong><span> During this window, all read requests from that user are dynamically routed to the Primary database instead of a replica.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;text-align: justify">The High-Speed Library</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Even with multiple replicas, hitting a database for every single page load is an expensive operation.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Databases must read data from a disk or a large memory pool and often perform complex joins between different tables to assemble a single record. To provide the millisecond response times neighbors expect, Nextdoor implemented a caching layer using Valkey. This is an open-source high-performance data store that holds information in RAM for near-instant access.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The team uses a Look-aside Cache pattern. When the application needs data, it follows a specific sequence:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong>The Cache Check:</strong><span> The application looks for the data in Valkey using a unique key.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong>The Cache Hit:</strong><span> If the data is found, it is returned instantly to the user without touching the database.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong>The Cache Miss:</strong><span> If the data is missing, the application queries the PostgreSQL database to find the truth.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong>The Population Step:</strong><span> The application takes the database result, saves a copy in Valkey for future requests, and then returns it to the user.</span></p></li></ul><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table
