justify">Efficiency is vital when managing a cache at this scale. RAM is much more expensive than disk storage, so the data must be as small as possible.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Nextdoor uses a binary serialization format called MessagePack. In other words, instead of storing data as a bulky text format like JSON, they convert it into a highly compressed binary format that is much faster for the computer to parse.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">MessagePack is particularly useful for Nextdoor because it supports schema evolution. If the engineering team adds a new field to a neighbor’s profile, the older cached data can still be read without crashing the application. For even larger pieces of data, they use Zstd compression. By combining these two tools, Nextdoor reduces the memory footprint of its cache servers.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;text-align: justify">Versioning and Atomic Updates</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Caching can create a serious problem when it starts lying in particular scenarios. For example, if the database is updated but the cache is not refreshed, users can see old, incorrect information. Most simple caching strategies rely on a “Time to Live” or TTL. This is a timer that tells the cache to delete an entry after a few minutes. For a real-time social network, waiting several minutes for a post to update is not an acceptable solution.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Nextdoor built a sophisticated versioning engine to ensure the cache stays up to date. They added a special column called system_version to their database tables and used PostgreSQL Triggers to manage this number. For reference, a trigger is a small script that runs automatically inside the database whenever a row is touched. Every time a post is updated, the trigger increments the version number. This ensures that the database remains the ultimate source of truth regarding which version of a post is the newest.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">When the application tries to update the cache, it does not just overwrite the old data. It uses a Lua script executed inside Valkey. This script performs an atomic Compare and set operation that works as follows:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong>The Metadata Fetch:</strong><span> The script retrieves the version number currently stored in the cache entry.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong>The Version Comparison:</strong><span> It compares the version to the version number of the new update being sent by the application.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong>The Conditional Write:</strong><span> If the new version is strictly greater than the cached version, the update is saved.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong>The Rejection:</strong><span> If the cached version is already equal to or higher than the new update, the script rejects the change entirely.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">This prevents “race conditions.” Imagine two different servers trying to update the same post at the same time. Without this logic, an older update could arrive a millisecond later and overwrite a newer update. This would leave the cache permanently out of sync with the database. By using Lua, the entire process of checking the version and updating the data happens as a single, unbreakable step that cannot be interrupted.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;text-align: justify">CDC and Reconciliation</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Even with versioning and Lua scripts, errors can occur.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">A network partition might prevent a cache update from reaching Valkey, or an application process might crash before it can finish the population step. Nextdoor needed a final safety net to catch these discrepancies. They implemented Change Data Capture, also known as CDC, using a tool called Debezium.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">See the diagram below:</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table works by “listening” to the internal logs of the PostgreSQL database. Specifically, it watches the Write-Ahead Log, where every single change is recorded before it is committed. Every time a change happens in the database, Debezium captures that event and turns it into a message in a data stream. A background service known as the Reconciler watches this stream.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The reconciliation flow provides a “self-healing” mechanism for the entire setup:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong>The Database Update:</strong><span> A user updates their neighborhood bio in the Primary PostgreSQL database.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong>The Log Capture:</strong><span> Debezium detects the new log entry and publishes a change event message.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong>The Reconciler Action:</strong><span> The background service receives this message and identifies which cache key needs to be corrected.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong>The Invalidation:</strong><span> The service tells the cache to delete the old entry. The next time a neighbor requests that bio, the application will experience a “Cache Miss” and fetch the perfectly fresh data from the database.</span></p></li></ul><div style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">This process provides eventual consistency. While the primary cache update might fail for a fraction of a second, the CDC Reconciler will eventually detect the change and fix the cache. It acts like a detective that constantly audits the system to ensure the fast truth in the cache matches the real truth in the database.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;text-align: justify">Sharding</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">There comes a point where even the most optimized single Primary database cannot handle the volume of incoming writes. When a platform processes billions of rows, the hardware itself reaches physical limits. This is when Nextdoor moves to the final rung of the ladder. This rung is Sharding.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Sharding is the process of breaking a single, massive table into smaller pieces and spreading them across entirely different database clusters. Nextdoor typically shards data by a unique identifier such as a Neighborhood ID.</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong>The Cluster Split:</strong><span> All data for Neighborhoods 1 through 500 might live on Cluster A, while Neighborhoods 501 through 1,000 live on Cluster B.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong>The Shard Key:</strong><span> The application uses the neighborhood_id to know exactly which database cluster to talk to for any given request.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Sharding allows for much greater scaling because we can keep adding more clusters based on growth. However, it comes at a high cost in complexity. Once we shard a database, we can no longer easily perform a “Join” between data on two different shards.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;text-align: justify">Conclusion</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The journey of Nextdoor’s database shows that great engineering is rarely about choosing the most complex tool first. It is about a disciplined progression.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">They started with a single server and added connection pooling when the lines got too long. They added replicas when the read traffic became too heavy. Finally, they built a world-class versioned caching system to provide the speed neighbors expect without sacrificing the accuracy they require.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The takeaway is that complexity must be earned. Each layer of the scaling ladder solves one problem while introducing a new challenge in data consistency. By building robust safety nets such as versioning and reconciliation, the Nextdoor engineering team ensured that its system could grow without losing the trust of the communities it serves.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><strong>References:</strong></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;margin-bottom: 0;"><li item.title: On The Socially Acceptable Use Of AI In Business
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
On The Socially Acceptable Use Of AI In Business

Dave Kellogg

“There’s a question I’ve been mulling for a while now, and I think it’s time to write it down: when is it okay to use generative AI in a given business context, and when does it cross a line? I’ll focus on two specific areas I know well — board work and strategic analysis — but I think the principles generalize.”

#Leadership Management
item.description: On The Socially Acceptable Use Of AI In Business

item.title: Encoding Team Standards
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Encoding Team Standards

Rahul Garg

““AI coding assistants respond to whoever is prompting, and the quality of what they produce depends on how well the prompter articulates team standards. I propose treating the instructions that govern AI interactions as infrastructure: versioned, reviewed, and shared artifacts that encode tacit team knowledge into executable instructions, making quality consistent regardless of who is at the keyboard.”

#Leadership Management
item.description: Encoding Team Standards

item.title: The Unwritten Laws Of Software Engineering
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
The Unwritten Laws Of Software Engineering

Anton Zaides

“As everybody and their mother thinks they can build great software right now, I decided to help them avoid a bit of pain. Here are 7 laws every engineer has broken at least once, learned the hard way.”

#BestPractices
item.description: The Unwritten Laws Of Software Engineering

item.title: Eight Years Of Wanting, Three Months Of Building With AI
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Eight Years Of Wanting, Three Months Of Building With AI

Lalit Maganti

“There’s no shortage of posts claiming that AI one-shot their project or pushing back and declaring that AI is all slop. I’m going to take a very different approach and, instead, systematically break down my experience building syntaqlite with AI, both where it helped and where it was detrimental.”

#Tools Productivity

Gergely Orosz

William Pliger

style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Giving an LLM more information can make it dumber. A</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2655b981-9c21-4ecd-98b6-97bd5df465b2?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: #7756e3;text-decoration: none;"> 2025 research study by Chroma</a><span> tested 18 of the most powerful language models available, including GPT-4.1, Claude, and Gemini, and found that every single one performed worse as the amount of input grew.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The degradation wasn’t minor, either. Some models held steady at 95% accuracy and then nosedived to 60% once the input crossed a certain length.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">This finding busts one of the most common myths about working with LLMs that more context is always better. The reality is that LLMs have architectural blind spots that make what you put in front of them, and how you structure it, far more important than how much you include.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The discipline of getting this right is called context engineering.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">In this article, we’ll look at how LLMs actually process the information you give them, what context engineering is, and the strategies that can help with it.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;text-align: justify">Key Terminologies</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Before we go further, there are three terms that come up constantly when talking about LLMs. Getting clear on these first will make everything that follows much easier to reason about.</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong>Tokens: </strong><span>They are the units LLMs think in. They aren’t full words, but rather chunks of text that average roughly three-quarters of a word each. The word “context” is one token, while the word “engineering” gets split into two. Every piece of text the model processes, from your question to its instructions to any documents you’ve included, is measured in tokens.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong>Context Window: </strong><span>It is the total number of tokens the model can see at once during a single interaction. Everything has to fit inside this window: the system instructions that define the model’s behavior, the conversation history, any external documents or data you’ve injected, and your actual question. Modern models advertise context windows ranging from 128,000 to over 2 million tokens. That sounds enormous, but as we’ll see, bigger isn’t straightforwardly better.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong>Attention: </strong><span>This is the mechanism the model uses to figure out which tokens matter to which other tokens. Before generating each new token of its response, the model compares it against every other token currently in the context window. This gives LLMs their ability to connect ideas across long stretches of text, but it’s also the source of their most important limitations.</span></p></li></ul><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;text-align: justify">How LLMs Process Context</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">When we send text to an LLM, it doesn’t read from top to bottom the way a human would. The attention mechanism compares every token against every other token to compute relationships, which means the model can, in principle, connect an idea from the first sentence of the input to one in the last sentence. However, this power comes with two critical costs.</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">The first is computational. Doubling the number of tokens in the context window roughly quadruples the computation required. Longer contexts are disproportionally slower and more expensive.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">The second cost is more consequential. Attention isn’t distributed evenly across the context window. Research has consistently shown that LLMs pay the most attention to tokens at the beginning and end of the input, with a significant drop-off in the middle. This is known as the “lost in the middle” problem, and research has found that accuracy can drop by over 30% when relevant information is placed in the middle of the input compared to the beginning or end.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">See the diagram below that shows the attention curve:</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">This isn’t a bug in any particular model, but rather a structural property of how transformers (the neural network architecture that powers virtually all modern LLMs) encode the position of tokens.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The positional encoding method used in most modern LLMs (called Rotary Position Embedding, or RoPE) introduces a decay effect that makes tokens far from both the start and end of the sequence land in a low-attention zone. Newer models have reduced the severity, but no production model has fully eliminated it.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The practical implication is that the position of information in the input matters as much as the information itself. If we paste a long document into an LLM, the model is most likely to miss information buried in the middle pages.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;text-align: justify">Why More Context Can Hurt</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The uneven attention distribution is one problem, but there’s a broader pattern that compounds it, known as context rot.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Context rot is the degradation of LLM performance as input length increases, even on simple tasks. The</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2655b981-9c21-4ecd-98b6-97bd5df465b2?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: #7756e3;text-decoration: none;"> Chroma research team’s 2025 study</a><span> tested 18 frontier models and found that this degradation isn’t gradual. Models can maintain near-perfect accuracy up to a certain context length, and then performance drops off a cliff unpredictably, varying by model and by task in ways that make it impossible to reliably predict when you’ll hit a breaking point.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Why does this happen?</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Every token you add to the context window draws from a finite attention budget. Irrelevant information buries important information in low-attention zones, and content that sounds related but isn’t actually useful confuses the model’s ability to identify what’s relevant. The model doesn’t get smarter with more input, but kind of gets distracted.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">On top of this, LLMs are stateless. They have zero memory between calls, and each interaction starts completely fresh. When there is a multi-turn conversation with an LLM like ChatGPT, and it seems to “remember” what we said earlier, that’s because the system is re-injecting the conversation history into the context window each time. The model itself remembers nothing, which means someone, or some system, has to decide for every single call what information to include, what to leave out, and how to structure it.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">There’s also a meaningful gap between marketing and reality. Models advertise million-token context windows, and they pass simple benchmarks at those lengths. However, the effective context length, where the model actually uses information reliably, is often much smaller. Passing a “needle in a haystack” test (finding one planted sentence in a long document) is very different from reliably synthesizing information scattered across hundreds of pages</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;text-align: justify">Defining Context Engineering</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Context engineering is the practice of designing, assembling, and managing the entire information environment an LLM sees before it generates a response. It goes beyond writing a single good instruction to orchestrating everything that fills the context window, so the model has exactly what it needs for the task at hand and nothing more.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">To understand what this involves, it helps to see what actually competes for space inside a context window. There are six types of context in a typical LLM call:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">System instructions (the behavioral rules, persona, and guidelines the model follows)</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">User input (your actual question or command)</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">Conversation history (the short-term memory of the current session)</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">Retrieved knowledge (documents, database results, or API responses pulled in from external sources)</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">Tool descriptions (definitions of tools the model can call and how to use them)</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">Tool outputs (results returned from previous tool calls)</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">The user’s actual question is often a tiny fraction of the total token count.</p></li></ul><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The rest is infrastructure, and that infrastructure is what context engineering designs.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">This also clarifies how context engineering differs from prompt engineering. Prompt engineering asks, “How do I phrase my instruction to get the best result?” On the other hand, Context engineering asks, “What does the model need to see right now, and how do I assemble all of it dynamically?”</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Prompt engineering is one component within context engineering, focused on the instruction layer, while context engineering encompasses the full information system around the model. As Andrej Karpathy put it in a</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4371032d-db68-4148-a18f-f35cb4877419?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: #7756e3;text-decoration: none;"> widely referenced post</a><span>, context engineering is the “delicate art and science of filling the context window with just the right information for the next step.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Two people using the same model can get wildly different results. The model is the same, but the context is different, and context engineering is the factor that determines things.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;text-align: justify">Core Strategies</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Developers have converged on four broad strategies for managing context,</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/79996cef-72af-41c0-a15d-0472278a31be?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: #7756e3;text-decoration: none;"> categorized </a><span>as write, select, compress, and isolate. Each one is a direct response to a specific constraint we’ve already covered.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.375em;text-align: justify">Write: Save Context Externally</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The constraint it addresses is that the context window is finite, and statelessness means information is lost between calls.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Instead of trying to keep everything inside the context window, save important information to external storage and bring it back when needed. This takes two main forms.</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The first is scratchpads, where an agent saves intermediate plans, notes, or reasoning steps to external storage during a long-running task.</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b09ebe3d-dff8-44a4-8928-666b44456634?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: #7756e3;text-decoration: none;"> Anthropic’s multi-agent research system</a><span> does exactly this. The lead researcher agent writes its plan to external memory at the start of a task, because if the context window exceeds 200,000 tokens, it gets truncated and the plan would be lost.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">The second form is long-term memory, which involves persisting information across sessions. ChatGPT auto-generates user preferences from conversations, Cursor and Windsurf learn coding patterns and project context, and Claude Code uses CLAUDE.md files as persistent instruction memory. All of these systems treat external storage as the real memory layer, with the context window serving as a temporary workspace.</p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.375em;text-align: justify">Select: Pull In Only What’s Relevant</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The constraint it addresses is that more context isn’t better, and the model needs the right information rather than all available information.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The most important technique here is Retrieval-Augmented Generation, or RAG. Instead of stuffing all your knowledge into the context window, we store it externally in a searchable database. At query time, retrieve only the chunks most relevant to the current question and inject those into the context, giving the model targeted knowledge without the noise of everything else.</p><div justify">Selection also applies to tools. When an agent has dozens of available tools, listing every tool description in every prompt wastes tokens and confuses the model. A better approach is to retrieve only the tool descriptions relevant to the current task.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The critical tradeoff with selection is precision. If the retrieval pulls in documents that are almost relevant but not quite, they become distractors that add tokens and push important context into low-attention zones. The retrieval step itself has to be good, or the whole strategy backfires.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.375em;text-align: justify">Compress: Keep Only What You Need</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The constraint it addresses is the context rot and the escalating cost of attention across more tokens.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">As agent workflows span dozens or hundreds of steps, the context window fills up with accumulated conversation history and tool outputs. Compression strategies reduce this bulk while trying to preserve the essential information.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Conversation summarization is the most common approach. Claude Code, for instance, triggers an “auto-compact” process when the context hits 95% capacity, summarizing the entire interaction history into a shorter form. Cognition, the company behind the Devin coding agent,</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/79996cef-72af-41c0-a15d-0472278a31be?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: #7756e3;text-decoration: none;"> trained a separate, dedicated model specifically for summarization</a><span> at agent-to-agent boundaries. The fact that they built a separate model just for this step tells us how consequential bad compression can be, since a specific decision or detail that gets summarized away is gone permanently.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Simpler forms of compression include trimming (removing older messages from the history) and tool output compression (reducing verbose search results or code outputs to their essentials before they enter the context).</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.375em;text-align: justify">Isolate: Split Context Across Agents</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The constraint it addresses is that of attention dilution and context poisoning when too many types of information compete in one window.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Instead of one agent trying to handle everything in a single bloated context window, this strategy splits the work across multiple specialized agents, each with its own clean, focused context. A “researcher” agent gets a context loaded with search tools and retrieved documents, while a “writer” agent gets a context loaded with style guides and formatting rules, so neither is distracted by the other’s information.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b09ebe3d-dff8-44a4-8928-666b44456634?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: #7756e3;text-decoration: none;">Anthropic demonstrated this with their multi-agent research system</a><span>, where a lead Opus 4 agent delegated sub-tasks to Sonnet 4 sub-agents. The system achieved a 90.2% improvement over a single Opus 4 agent on research tasks, despite using the same underlying model family. The entire performance gain came from how context was managed, not from a more powerful model.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">See the diagram below:</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;text-align: justify">Tradeoffs</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">These strategies are powerful, but they involve trade-offs with no universal right answers:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong>Compression versus information loss:</strong><span> Every time you summarize, you risk losing a detail that turns out to matter later. The more aggressively you compress, the more you save on tokens, but the higher the chance of permanently destroying something important.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong>Single agent versus multi-agent:</strong><span> Anthropic’s multi-agent results are impressive, but others,</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/79996cef-72af-41c0-a15d-0472278a31be?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: #7756e3;text-decoration: none;"> notably Cognition</a><span>, have argued that a single agent with good compression delivers more stability and lower cost. Both sides are debating the same core question of how to manage context effectively, and the answer depends on task complexity, cost tolerance, and reliability requirements.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong>Retrieval precision versus noise:</strong><span> RAG adds knowledge, but imprecise retrieval adds distractors. If the documents you retrieve aren’t genuinely relevant, they consume tokens and push important content into low-attention positions, so the retrieval system itself has to be well-engineered, or RAG makes things worse.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong>Cost versus richness:</strong><span> Every token costs money and processing time. The disproportionate scaling of attention means longer contexts get expensive fast, and context engineering is partly an economics problem of figuring out where the return on additional tokens stops being worth the cost.</span></p></li></ul><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;text-align: justify">Conclusion</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The core takeaway is that the model is only as good as the context it receives. Working with LLMs effectively requires thinking about the entire system around the model, not just the model itself.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">As models get more powerful, context engineering becomes more important. When the model is capable enough, most failures stop being intelligence failures and start being context failures, where the model could have gotten it right but didn’t have what it needed or had too much of what it didn’t need.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The strategies are evolving, and best practices are being revised as new models ship. However, the underlying constraints of finite attention, positional bias, and statelessness are architectural.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>References</strong></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;margin-bottom: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.375em;">Stream of GitHub outages from infra overload</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>GitHub’s CTO, Vladimir Fedorov, addressed availability issues </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0b7ffe77-ff01-4e01-88a5-d98ed516cf85?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">in a blog post</a><span> and covered three major incidents:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f144a176-a178-44fa-8448-638b9cf20dfa?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">2 February</a><span>: security policies unintentionally blocked access to virtual machine metadata</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e253babd-95f9-44fa-984d-7d87fb627780?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">9 February</a><span>: a database cluster got overloaded</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d0c1857a-385d-4d41-909c-a9de82b4c9d7?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">5 March</a><span>: writes failed on a Redis cluster</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Software engineer Lori Hochstein did </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e61aa038-2e93-4a4a-be8c-db9f33a56030?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">a helpful analysis</a><span> of these outages and the CTO’s response, and has interesting observations:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Saturation</strong><span>: the database cluster incident (9 Feb) was a case of the database getting saturated, due to higher-than-expected usage. Databases are harder to scale up than stateless services. GitHub also underestimated how much additional traffic there would be.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Failover + telemetry gap</strong><span>: the 2 Feb incident was a combination of an infra issue in one region failing over to a healthy region, and making things worse with a telemetry gap (incorrect security policies were applied in the new regions which blocked access to VM metadata)</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Failover + configuration issue</strong><span>: the 5 March incident was uncannily similar: after a failover, a configuration issue blocked writes on a Redis cluster</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It is certainly nice to get details from GitHub on these outages. It feels to me that infra strains are causing more infra issues → they trigger constraints faster → failovers are not as smooth as they should be. Could it be because GitHub keeps changing their existing systems?</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.375em;">Startup shows GitHub how it’s done</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>While GitHub struggles to keep up with the increase in load from AI agents generating more code and pull requests, a new startup called Pierre Computer claims to have built an “AI-native” solution for AI agents pushing code, which scales far beyond what GitHub can do. Pierre was founded by </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9b29f7eb-e1e2-4382-89f7-c5f121304831?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Jacob Thornton</a><span>: formerly an engineer at Coinbase, Medium, and Twitter, and also the creator of the once-very popular </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a3d27091-da7a-4552-b420-5585182d3d20?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Bootstrap</a><span> CSS library.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Here’s what Pierre supports, which GitHub does not:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">“In October [2025], Github shared they were averaging ~230 new repos per minute.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Last week we [at Pierre Computer] hit a sustained peak of > 15,000 repos per minute for 3 hours.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And in the last 30 days customers have created > 9M repos”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>These are incredible numbers – if also self-reported – and something that GitHub clearly cannot get close to, at least not today! There are few details about customers, while the product – called </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5d59484d-61b7-40fd-b33d-60659740038b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Code.storage</a><span> – seems to be in closed beta.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Still, this is the type of “git for AI agents” that GitHub has failed to build, and the type of infrastructure it needs badly.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.375em;">Has GitHub lost focus and purpose?</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">GitHub’s reliability issues are acute enough that, if it keeps up, teams will start giving alternatives like small startups such as Pierre a try, or perhaps even consider self-hosting Git. But how did the largest Git host in the world neglect its customers, and fail to prepare its infra for an increase in code commits and pull requests?</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Mitchell Hashimoto, founder of Ghostty, and a heavy user of GitHub himself, had advice on what he would do if he was in charge of GitHub, after growing frustrated with the state of its core offering. He </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/eac2c9ac-77e5-463d-a5f1-98db7bad099d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">writes</a><span> (emphasis mine)</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">“Here’s what I’d do if I was in charge of GitHub, in order:</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>1. Establish a North Star plan around being critical infrastructure for agentic code</strong><span> lifecycles and determine a set of ways to measure that.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>2. Fire everyone who works on or advocates for Copilot and shut it down.</strong><span> It’s not about the people, I’m sure there’s many talented people; you’re just working at the wrong company.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>3. Buy Pierre and launch agentic repo hosting as the first agentic product.</strong><span> Repos would be separate from the legacy web product to start, since they’re likely burdened with legacy cross product interactions.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>4. Re-evaluate all product lines and initiatives against the new North Star. </strong><span>I suspect 50% get cut (to make room for different ones).</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The big idea is all agentic interactions should critically rely on GitHub APIs. Code review should be agentic but the labs should be building that into GH (not bolted in through GHA like today, real first class platform primitives). GH should absolutely launch an agent chat primitive, agent mailboxes are obviously good. GH should be a platform and not an agent itself.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This is going to be very obviously lacking since I only have external ideas to work off of and have no idea how GitHub internals are working, what their KPIs are or what North Star they define, etc.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But, with imperfect information, this is what I’d do.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">My sense is that GitHub has three concurrent problems:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>GitHub and Copilot are entangled with Microsoft’s internal politics. </strong><span>GitHub’s Copilot in 2021 was the first massively successful “AI product.” Microsoft took the “Copilot” brand and used it across all of their product lines, creating low-quality AI integrations. Simultaneously, internal Microsoft orgs like Azure and Microsoft AI were trying to get their hands on GitHub, which is one of the most positive developer brands at Microsoft.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>GitHub has no leader, seemingly by design. </strong><span>GitHub’s last CEO was Thomas Dohmke, who stepped down voluntarily, and Microsoft never backfilled the CEO role; instead carrying out a reorg to make GitHub part of Microsoft’s AI group and stripping its independence. It seems the “Microsoft AI” side won that battle.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>GitHub has no focus, and is stuck chasing Copilot as a revenue source. </strong><span>GitHub has no CEO and is caught up in internal politics, so, what can GitHub teams do? The safest bet is to increase revenue and the best way to do that is by investing more into GitHub Copilot, and ignoring long-term issues like reliability.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I agree with Mitchell: GitHub has no “North Star” and we see a large org being dysfunctional. That lack of vision – and CEO – is hitting hard:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">GitHub Copilot went from the most-used AI agent in 2021, to be overtaken by Claude Code, and is soon to be overtaken by Cursor.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">As a platform, GitHub has no vision for how to evolve to support AI agents. Sure, GitHub has an MCP server, but it has no “AI-native git platform” that can handle the massive load AI agents generate.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>GitHub keeps shipping small features and improvements without direction. For example, in October 2025, they </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/59c9db93-1b0d-4f55-8910-dacd7f9357da?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">started to work on</a><span> stacked diffs. However, when it ships, the stacked diffs workflow might be mostly obsolete – at least with AI agents!</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It’s easy to win a market when you do one thing better than anyone else in the world. Right now, GitHub is doing too many things and doing a subpar job with Copilot, its platform, and AI infra.</p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Read the full issue of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fac4c45d-d940-46a9-8271-e4481891a692?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">last week’s The Pulse</a><span>, or check out </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b8b7a902-41c8-4e24-a0e7-0da3982af74a?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">this week’s The Pulse</a><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Catch up with recent The Pragmatic Engineer issues:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;margin-bottom: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/86cd445a-af5c-4051-b040-6fd7bd663944?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Scaling Uber with Thuan Pham</a></strong><span> (Uber’s first CTO — podcast). We went into topics like scaling Uber from constant outages to global infrastructure, the shift to microservices and platform teams, and how AI is reshaping engineering.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7807fb0d-22cc-428f-8848-da513b7ac5f4?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Building WhatsApp with Jean Lee</a></strong><span> (podcast): Jean Lee, engineer #19 at WhatsApp, on scaling the app with a tiny team, the Facebook acquisition, and what it reveals about the future of engineering.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6d1c84ac-d5d3-4b5f-b1f8-2ef55a901cc5?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">What will the Staff Engineer role look like in 2027 and beyond</a><span>?</span></strong><span> What happens to the Staff engineer role when agents write more code? April 3rd, 2026   |   Read online

Friday 3rd March issue is presented by SerpApi

SerpApi: The Ultimate Sidekick For Your AI Applications

AI is smarter when it can search the web. How are AI companies doing it? Meet the worst-kept secret in the AI industry: the SerpApi web search API:
👉 Scrape Google and other search engines (including AI overviews, Maps, Shopping, Amazon, and more)
👉 Integrate with a dead-simple GET request that any agent can make.
👉 Used by NVIDIA, Uber, Adobe, and even the United Nations.

Give it a try now; no sign-up needed.

Explore our Playground

 

I’m An Introvert. This Is How I Get Myself To Speak Up.

— Wes Kao

tl;dr: I often get readers who ask, “Wes, if I’m not naturally loud, how do I speak up or talk about my accomplishments? How do I gain more visibility, either internally in my company or externally online?”

CareerAdvice
 

What Kinds Of New Debt Are Teams Accumulating With AI?

— Lizzie Matusov

tl;dr: Dr. Margaret-Anne Storey at the University of Victoria proposes a “triple debt model” for reasoning about software system health, drawing on recent empirical research on developer cognition, AI-assisted development, and software evolution. The paper is a conceptual framework, not a controlled experiment - it synthesizes findings across multiple studies to argue that technical debt alone is an incomplete lens.

Leadership Management
 

The Ultimate Sidekick for Your AI Applications

tl;dr: AI is smarter when it can search the web. How are AI companies doing it? Meet the worst-kept secret in the AI industry: the SerpApi web search API: (1) Scrape Google and other search engines (including AI overviews, Maps, Shopping, Amazon, and more). (2) Integrate with a dead-simple GET request that any agent can make. (3) Used by NVIDIA, Uber, Adobe, and even the United Nations.

Promoted by SerpApi

Tools
 

What I Learned From Nearly 1,000 Interviews At Amazon

— Steve Huynh

tl;dr: “A Bar Raiser is a specially trained interviewer whose job is to ensure that every hire raises the average talent level at Amazon. I had veto power over any candidate. I sat on nearly a thousand interview loops across every level from intern to Principal Engineer.” Steven discusses the patterns that emerged.

Leadership Management Hiring

“Whether you think you can or you think you can’t, you’re right.”

 
— Henry Ford

No Semicolons Needed

— Terts Diepraam

tl;dr: “I'm making a scripting language called Roto. Like so many programming languages before it, it has the goal of being easy to use and read. Many languages end up making semicolons to delimit or terminate statements optional to that end. I want that too!”

LanguageDesign
 

IaCConf: How Teams Manage IaC At Scale

tl;dr: Most IaC content focuses on theory. This virtual conference is different. IaCConf brings together engineers sharing what’s actually working in production - from scaling to managing complexity across teams. Real lessons from operators and practical patterns you can apply.

Promoted by Spacelift

Event
 

The Skill Of Using AI Agents Well

tl;dr: “What tips, tricks, approaches are you using to improve your efficiency when using agent harnesses? I personally focus on Claude Code & Codex CLI mostly for single person software development, but I welcome suggestions for other tools and other areas of use. Ideally you share what you tried and what works for you and I try it myself and see whether it improves my workflow. Here are my discoveries (with level of confidence).”

Agents
 

Reading Leaked Claude Code Source Code

tl;dr: “Anthropic accidentally leaked a source map file containing the full, unobfuscated TypeScript source code. 1,897 files around 132,000 LOC. What I found is a piece of software that is surprisingly more opinionated and more paranoid than I expected. Here are some of things that I found worth talking about.”

Claude Design
 

Architecture Decision Record

— Martin Fowler

tl;dr: “An Architecture Decision Record (ADR) is a short document that captures and explains a single decision relevant to a product or ecosystem. Documents should be short, just a couple of pages, and contain the decision, the context for making it, and significant ramifications. They should not be modified if the decision is changed, but linked to a superseding decision.”

Documentation
 

Null Pointer

Simple Request

Hand-drawn by Manu. Archives here.

 

Most Popular From Last Issue

Nobody Is Coming To Save Your Career - Steve Huynh

 

Notable Links

Claude Code (Thread): Collection of lesser-known features & workflows.

Hermes: Agent that grows with you.

Openscreen: OS alternative to screen studio.

Open Terminal: A computer you can curl.

Pg_textsearch: Modern ranked text search for Postgres.

The team is happy with the results. However, six months later, the main table has grown from 50,000 rows to 5 million, and the same query now takes eight seconds.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Then, someone adds an index, and read latency drops to milliseconds, which seems like a clear win. But a week later, the nightly data import is running 40% slower than before. Fixing one problem created another.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">This is the central challenge of database performance.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Every optimization helps one thing and can potentially hurt something else. Indexes speed up reads but slow down writes. Caching reduces database load but introduces stale data. Denormalization makes queries faster but complicates updates.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The real challenge isn’t knowing the strategies, but understanding what each strategy costs and deciding which tradeoffs a given application can afford. In this article, we’ll go through the major strategies for improving database performance along with their benefits and trade-offs.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size:
