auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table><figcaption class="image-caption" style="box-sizing: content-box;color: rgb(119,119,119);font-size: 14px;line-height: 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;"><em>A strong autoscaling system for inference matches resources to demand</em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Autoscaling systems use Kubernetes, an open-source container orchestration system, along with a cluster-level system for provisioning and deallocating compute. Kubernetes can run one or more replicas of a model container, each on its own instance. An instance includes the GPUs and other hardware resources that the container requires.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Unless your traffic is unusually consistent, there probably isn’t a specific number of replicas that perfectly matches your needs.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Autoscaling is the practice of dynamically adjusting the number of replicas allocated to a given model within a cluster. There are two ways to make autoscaling decisions:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Utilization:</strong><span> Scale up or down based on GPU utilization signals like memory usage or compute usage.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Traffic:</strong><span> Scale up and down based on the number of requests being processed in the system.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Utilization and traffic don’t always match. For example, in LLM prefill, a few requests with hundreds of thousands of uncached input tokens could cause much higher utilization than many small requests with high cache hit rates.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Traffic-based scaling decisions can be made proactively, while utilization is a lagging indicator. Use both in combination to keep system resources matched with demand.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">When designing a traffic-based autoscaling system, you want to configure five factors:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Min replicas:</strong><span> What is the minimum number of replicas that stay running, regardless of traffic?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Max replicas:</strong><span> What is the maximum number of replicas you can allocate when traffic is high?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Autoscaling window:</strong><span> How long is the sliding timeframe used to measure traffic and make autoscaling decisions?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Scale down delay:</strong><span> For how long after a scale-down is suggested do you wait, in case there’s another traffic spike?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Concurrency target:</strong><span> How many requests can each replica handle at once?</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The exact configuration determines how well the autoscaling system achieves its goals of maintaining latency SLAs without wasting resources. For example, increasing the scale-down delay prevents premature scaledowns for spikey traffic, but could result in unnecessary spend after traffic has properly cooled down.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Autoscaling within a single cluster works up to a certain point, but high-volume deployments serving a global user base need thousands of GPUs distributed around the world.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It’s straightforward to build multi-cloud inference as a collection of siloed compute across different cloud providers. But in these setups, there’s no way to use inter-cloud compute fluidly, and moving workloads across clouds is a tedious, error-prone process.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">True multi-cloud inference requires building a multi-region, multi-provider bin packing tool, which treats distinct pools of compute as fungible with each other. Like Kubernetes within a single cluster, multi-cloud capacity management must take a global view, enabling global scheduling.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" planes to a multi-cluster, multi-region system</em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Running true multi-cloud inference unlocks:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Capacity:</strong><span> Pool capacity from multiple providers for greater, more flexible GPU access.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Redundancy: </strong><span>Split inference across providers for resiliency against outages.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Latency:</strong><span> Run inference close to end users to reduce network latency overhead.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Compliance: </strong><span>Run inference in compliance with data sovereignty and other regulatory requirements.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Scaling from one cluster in one cloud to many clusters in many clouds requires a new coordination layer. A multi-cloud architecture contains:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Control plane:</strong><span> Handles model deployment and global scaling decisions, receives real-time event streams.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Workload planes:</strong><span> Handles direct inference traffic and in-cluster scaling decisions, reports utilization and demand.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This separation of responsibilities ensures that individual workload planes can serve traffic independently. If something happens to the control plane or any given workload plane, other workloads should be unaffected.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;">7. Five approaches to make inference faster</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">One of the coolest things about working in inference engineering is that, unlike many industries where new academic research takes years or decades to be adopted, techniques from new papers are live in production within months or even weeks.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But there is a gap to bridge between research and production, and some of the most visible inference engineering work of all comes from doing so.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Real-world traffic defies constraints. But with volume, you can adapt systems over time to match the changing nature of usage. Tuning the parameters of inference engines, speculation algorithms, and model servers isn’t a one-time task. Instead, either through iterative deployments or dynamic runtime adjustments, you can continuously improve the performance of an inference system.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Finding the right combination of techniques and configurations takes patient experimentation. I remember an internal hackathon during which one of Baseten’s inference engineers worked on an autocomplete model for code, and ended up trying 77 different configurations via a handwritten script before finding a non-obvious solution that doubled TPS (tokens per second) for a customer’s model.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Sometimes, techniques are symbiotic or incompatible, which makes inference optimization even more complex. For example, quantizing the KV cache alleviates a bottleneck in disaggregation, but increasing batch sizing reduces the compute available for speculation. An inference engineer’s challenge is always to create a balanced set of optimizations that delivers more than the sum of its parts.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Let’s look into the key categories of applied research for inference acceleration: quantization, speculation, caching, parallelism, and disaggregation.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.375em;">Approach #1: Quantization</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Quantization means reducing the numerical precision of a model’s weights. It improves latency (both TTFT [time to first token] and TPS, increases system throughput, and opens up headroom for other optimizations like disaggregation, speculation, and prefix caching to be even more effective. But when it goes wrong, quantization can materially reduce a model’s output quality.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Models are trained with weights, activations, and other components represented in a certain native number format. Usually, this is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a593b652-231f-44e7-bc93-d25050101981?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">BF16</a><span> or </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/afc54954-0ea2-41a1-935e-4f78d30898d1?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">FP16</a><span>, although 8-bit and 4-bit native precisions are becoming more popular for training.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Post-training quantization works by changing those model weights and other values from their native number format, to a lower-precision format. Cutting precision in half improves performance in both phases of inference:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Prefill: </strong><span>Compute-bound prefill now runs on lower-precision Tensor Cores with twice the FLOPS.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Decode: </strong><span>Memory-bound decode now loads half as much data per value, effectively doubling memory bandwidth.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Working with quantized data introduces overheads, so it’s not linearly twice as fast to go from 16 to 8 bits. In practice, quantization down a single level of precision generally offers 30%-50% better performance for LLMs. The catch with quantization is that it runs the risk of reducing a model’s output quality, and has the potential to introduce precision errors throughout the calculations that power inference.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Precision errors compound over time. Consider what happens when you square and cube different precisions of Pi:</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="902" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/0c65ec1f-11d6-47bc-9db9-0ae1b0a9d396?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="position: relative;flex-direction: column;align-items: center;padding: 0;width: auto;height: auto;border: none;text-decoration: none;display: block;margin: 0;"><img class="wide-image" auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Most of the work in quantization is in preventing precision errors and minimizing their impact on the final model output.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Sixteen-bit, 8-bit, and 4-bit precisions are the primary formats for inference. Number formats contain:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Precision:</strong><span> The number of bits used to express a single value in the format. For example, FP16 uses 16 bits.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Type:</strong><span> Whether these bits are interpreted to represent an integer (non decimal) or a floating-point number (decimal).</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Scale factor:</strong><span> A multiplier used to map values from a low-precision format back to the higher-precision format.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Combined, these attributes determine the two factors behind how well a number format represents the values used in inference:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Dynamic range:</strong><span> The difference between the lowest and highest value that can be represented in the format.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Granularity:</strong><span> The number of parameters or other values that are quantized along a single scale factor.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Dynamic range is essential to low-precision inference without quality loss. Sixteen bits can represent 65,536 distinct values, while 8 bits can only represent 256 different values. The dynamic range is the distribution of these values – the difference between the smallest and largest available value.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Dynamic range explains why floating-point formats are better than integer formats for inference. Floating-point formats have three properties:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Sign: </strong><span>A single bit that represents whether a number is positive or negative.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Exponent: </strong><span>A set of bits that, taken together, represent an exponent factor.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Mantissa: </strong><span>A set of bits that together represent the base value multiplied by two to the exponent.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">An FP8 number in an E4M3 data format means it has a 4-bit exponent and a 3-bit mantissa, with the remaining bit for the sign. Integer formats only have sign and value bits.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table><figcaption class="image-caption" style="box-sizing: content-box;color: rgb(119,119,119);font-size: 14px;line-height: 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;"><em>Floating-point number formats have exponent and mantissa bits, along with the sign bit</em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The exponent in floating-point numbers gives it a higher dynamic range, meaning it can better express very large and very small numbers. This is important because outlier values are significant in inference, and floating-point number formats better represent outliers after quantization.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Within floating-point formats, there are multiple options at each precision, like FP4, MXFP4, and NVFP4. These formats differ in granularity, or in the number of values quantized by a single scale factor.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Quantization can be applied at three levels:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Tensor level: </strong><span>Calculate a single scale factor for the entire QKV tensor.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Channel level: </strong><span>Calculate a different scale factor for each feature vector within the tensor.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Block level: </strong><span>Within each feature vector, divide the vector into blocks of N values and calculate a scale factor for each block.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">More granular quantization has a lower chance of smoothing over outliers, which preserves quality. However, more granularity also introduces extra overhead for storing and applying scale factors.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The components of a model have varying sensitivities to quantization. Reducing the precision of more sensitive components runs a higher risk of quality degradation. From the least to most sensitive components:</p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Weights: </strong><span>the linear layers are least sensitive to quantization.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Activations: </strong><span>The intermediate output of activation functions are only somewhat sensitive to quantization. They are rarely quantized as they are such a tiny fraction of the model’s weights.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>KV cache: </strong><span>The cached values from the attention calculation are moderately sensitive to quantization.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Attention: </strong><span>The attention layers of a model are highly sensitive to quantization, especially equations like softmax.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Within each component, you can get more selective about quantization.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Even in linear layers and activations – generally the least sensitive to quantization due to their size – early and late layers, like the input and output layers of the neural network, may be left in their original precision as these layers are more sensitive.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">While quantizing weights and activations helps performance, KV cache quantization gives an additional boost to techniques like prefix caching and disaggregation. The KV cache is a valuable resource and quantizing it allows inference engines to store more of it in memory and read it more quickly.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">However, the KV cache for each token is used by each subsequent token. This means precision errors introduced by quantization can compound from token to token. Compounding errors are exactly why attention layers are the riskiest to quantize: not only is attention very sensitive to dynamic range, but each attention calculation relies on the results of each previous attention calculation. Therefore, over a sequence of thousands of tokens, errors accumulate quickly.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">All but the most aggressive quantization schemes run functions like softmax in their original precision.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure KV cache, and high for attention</em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">A moderate approach to low-precision inference uses a format like FP8 with high dynamic range – if possible, a microscaling format like MXFP8 – to carefully quantize select linear layers, activations, and often KV cache values. Even with these high dynamic range formats, components of the attention layer are rarely quantized.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.375em;">Approach #2: Speculative decoding</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The decode phase of LLM inference is an autoregressive process in which tokens are generated one at a time. The bottleneck on decode is memory bandwidth, with compute sitting idle at low-to-moderate batch sizes as weights are read from memory.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Speculative decoding takes advantage of that spare compute to try and generate multiple tokens per forward pass through the target model. If an inference engine could generate two, three, or even more tokens for each round-trip of weights through memory, it would generate far more tokens per second. Note, speculative decoding only improves TPS / ITL (inter-token latency), not TTFT (time to first token.)</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">There are multiple algorithms for speculative decoding and they share a common mechanism:</p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The speculator generates one or more </span><strong>draft tokens</strong><span>.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The </span><strong>target model</strong><span> – or the underlying model that you’re trying to accelerate – performs </span><strong>validation</strong><span> on these tokens to check if they match what the model would generate.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">The target model accepts any valid draft tokens and generates an additional token itself, completing the forward pass.</p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This generates N+1 tokens per forward pass, or iteration through the decode loop, where N is the number of accepted draft tokens.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Generating draft tokens is not free, it takes both compute and memory. However, it is much faster for a target model to validate a draft token than to generate an original token. If you imagine a sudoku puzzle, solving it is hard, but checking if the solution is correct is very easy. For the target model, generating a token is like solving a sudoku, while validating a draft token is like checking a finished sudoku.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The performance uplift from any speculative decoding strategy depends on three factors:</p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Draft token cost: </strong><span>Time taken to generate a draft token.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Draft sequence length: </strong><span>The number of draft tokens generated per forward pass.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Token acceptance rate:</strong><span> The percentage of draft tokens accepted by the target model.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Token acceptance rate is high early in the draft sequence, but draft tokens get less reliable deeper in the sequence.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;">Speculative decoding from draft token generation and validation to prefix acceptance with subsequent token generation</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Aim for short, high-percentage sequences</strong><span> because while generating and validating tokens is inexpensive relative to generating tokens in the original model, it still comes with meaningful overhead. Additionally, once a single draft token is rejected as wrong, all subsequent tokens in the sequence are also rejected.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Working with speculation is interesting because so many factors affect token acceptance rate. The big one is the temperature parameter – higher temperatures yield token distributions that are harder to predict, reducing the effectiveness of speculative decoding. But even factors as simple as subject matter can make a difference on acceptance rate if the draft model or additional decoder head used for speculation is better versed in, say, math than history.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Another limitation on speculative decoding is that it’s most useful at low batch sizes where there are spare compute cycles. At higher batch sizes, speculative decoding must be dynamically disabled as compute is too saturated to afford verification.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Each speculation algorithm navigates these tradeoffs differently, and careful implementation of the right algorithm for the situation can lead to major improvements in TPS.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.375em;">Approach #3: Caching</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">During prefill, the inference engine builds a KV cache (a store of keys and values for each token) on the input sequence. It then updates the KV cache for each token during decode. As inference is autoregressive, the value for each new token depends on the value of every previous token in the sequence.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Every inference engine uses KV caching by default on a request-by-request basis. Without KV caching, LLM inference would be unbearably slow since each previous value in the entire sequence would need to be recalculated for each subsequent token.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">However, engineers can get more utility from the KV cache by reusing it between requests rather than solely within each inference sequence.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Consider the following two prompts, each with four tokens on most tokenizers:</p><div prefixes</em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">By default, the inference engine has to run prefill on all four tokens of each prompt. But the first tokens of each prompt – “Weather in” – form a shared prefix between the pair.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">With prefix caching, you can reuse the KV cache from the first request to improve TTFT on the second request by skipping prefill on the first two tokens and reading in the existing KV cache instead.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">When you see pay-per-token APIs charge less for “cache hit” input tokens than “cache miss” tokens, this is why: reusing cached tokens takes very little compute power and time. As an inference engineer, you can apply the same principle to reduce latency, improve throughput and therefore save money on your own deployments.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Saving two tokens won’t make a big impact on TTFT, but prefix caching can skip prefill on thousands of tokens in certain domains:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Complex system prompts: </strong><span>Agents, customer-facing chatbots, RAG scaffolds, and tool calls often feature long, complex system prompts on every call.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Code completion: </strong><span>Code completion, code generation, and other coding functions require passing the same thousands of lines of code as shared context.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Documents and retrieval: </strong><span>Document summarization, question answering, and retrieval all add repeated context ahead of user prompts.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Multi-turn conversations: </strong><span>Ordinary conversations repeat back every message in a chat template, increasing the savings from prefix caching with every turn.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Prefix caching works from the start of the input sequence until the first non-repeated token. The fourth token in the weather example, a question mark, is shared between the two input sequences. However, the prefix ends at the first non-repeated token, so the fourth token isn’t read from cache.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Since prefixes end at the first unique token, your context engineering determines TTFT savings. Consider a different approach to the same prompt:</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.375em;">Approach #5: Disaggregation</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Disaggregation combines three important ideas in inference engineering:</p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Prefill is a compute-bound process that determines the time to first token (TTFT), while decode is a memory-bound process that determines TPS.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Specialization improves performance in everything from kernel selection to inference engine parameter tuning.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">You can effectively parallelize model serving over multiple GPUs, or even multiple nodes, if you can avoid bottlenecks from lower-bandwidth interconnects.</p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">When prefill and decode run on the same node under heavy traffic, they have a higher chance of interfering with one another. Ideally, prefill uses more compute resources, while decode uses more memory, and the two can co-exist efficiently. However, with larger batches and more compute-intensive optimizations, prefill and decode start competing for resources.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Disaggregation, or disaggregated serving, is the idea of separating prefill and decode into separate engines on separate GPUs or nodes.</p><div auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table><figcaption class="image-caption" style="box-sizing: content-box;color: rgb(119,119,119);font-size: 14px;line-height: 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;">Disaggregation assigns prefill workers to generate the first token and decode workers to generate subsequent tokens</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Disaggregation turns LLM inference into a three-step process:</p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">The prefill engine takes the input sequence and generates a KV cache while computing the first token.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">The prefill engine sends the KV cache over the hardware interconnect to the decode engine.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">The decode engine computes all subsequent tokens.</p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In conditional disaggregation, the request is first sent to the decode engine, which checks if the input sequence is already cached, or is short enough to handle locally:</p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">If so, the decode engine handles prefill locally, skipping disaggregation.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">If not, the decode engine transfers the request to the prefill engine for disaggregated serving.</p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Conditional disaggregation is better for real-world traffic.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Another benefit of disaggregation is that with separate prefill and decode engines, you can optimize each engine individually and the system as a whole. For example, the compute-bound prefill engine requires a lower TP than the memory-bound decode engine.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro underline;">waitlist</a><span> to be notified when it’s available.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>It’s encouraging that inference engineering is no longer a “monopoly” belonging to a few leading AI labs. </strong><span>Top AI model makers like OpenAI and Anthropic control all aspects of their AI models – from training to inference – so there’s no inference engineering to be done with them.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">However, thanks to increasingly capable open models, engineering teams have the opportunity to tweak how they use models, and this is where the theory and practice of inference engineering becomes invaluable.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Even so, the discipline of inference engineering still seems to only make sense for a subset of tech companies. </strong><span>To justify investment in inference engineering, you need to be spending big money on inference from vendors. This is the point at which it can make sense to invest time and money to see if you can set up your own inference stack on top of open models, and swap out some existing usage.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>I wonder if inference engineering is the AI version of the “build vs buy” dilemma. </strong><span>For software-as-a-service (SaaS), the question for every company is whether to build it in-house, or buy from a vendor. For example, should you build a project management software (it’s possible!), or just buy an existing one? And what about feature flagging, not to mention observability?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Experienced engineers all understand the pros and cons of building it yourself (time and maintenance, which is a constant drag.) Tuning and operating your own LLM stack is a much newer field, and inference engineering is at the heart of building better inference stacks than what comes “out of the box” with open models.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><strong>Picking up the basics of inference engineering feels like a valuable skill – and it’s also new and interesting. </strong><span>If you become well-versed in inference engineering, you could create optionality for your own team and company in LLM usage</span><strong>. </strong><span>Running your own inference stack on top of an open model gives control of what you’re running and of pricing. Inference engineering helps create options for achieving better performance from an open model by using the approaches covered in the extract above from Philip’s book.</span></p></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;word-break: break-word;margin-bottom: 16px;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>You’re on the free list for </em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9uZXdzbGV0dGVyLnByYWdtYXRpY2VuZ2luZWVyLmNvbT91dG1fY2FtcGFpZ249ZW1haWwtaG9tZSZyPTM2eGwxbyIsInAiOjE5Mjc1MzIzNywicyI6NDU4NzA5LCJmIjp0cnVlLCJ1IjoxOTMwNDMxNDgsImlhdCI6MTc3NDk3NjgzMSwiZXhwIjoyMDkwNTUyODMxLCJpc3MiOiJwdWItMCIsInN1YiI6ImxpbmstcmVkaXJlY3QifQ.LaayztJ5Y0tDqPX0t4jFIw2qPOQW1_PPATzul-VonyM?" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">The Pragmatic Engineer</a><em><span>. style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Every growing engineering organization eventually discovers the same problem. When something breaks in production, engineers debug it. When it breaks again, they debug it again. Hundreds of teams, thousands of incidents, each one investigated mostly from scratch.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The experienced engineer knows where to look and what patterns to check, but that knowledge lives in their head, not in the system. Over time, runbooks go stale, and scripts that one person wrote become tribal knowledge.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Meta hit this wall years ago. Their answer was DrP, a platform that lets engineers turn investigation expertise into actual code. It is a software component that runs automatically, gets tested through code review, and improves over time. It now runs across 300 teams and executes 50,000 automated analyses daily.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">While Meta’s specific tool is interesting to learn about, even more insightful is the underlying principle that debugging itself can be engineered. In this article, we will look at how DrP works on a high level and the design choices Meta made while building it.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><em>Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from the Meta Engineering Team. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.</em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;text-align: justify">Why Manual Investigation Breaks Down</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The way most teams investigate incidents has a predictable failure mode, and writing better documentation doesn’t fix it.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Knowledge is trapped in people. Your best debugger carries mental models nobody else has, such as which services are flaky, which metrics actually matter, and which dashboards lie under certain conditions. When that person is asleep, on vacation, or leaves the company, the knowledge is gone. If you’ve ever been paged at 2 AM and wished someone had already figured this out last time it happened, you’ve felt this problem.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Systems change frequently, sometimes dozens of times a day. The runbook that was accurate last month now references a dashboard that was renamed and a service that was refactored. Modern software moves too fast for static documentation to keep up.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Teams often write one-off scripts to automate their own checks, and that’s a good thing to have. But those scripts can’t cross service boundaries. Neither are they tested systematically. Ultimately, they become their own form of tribal knowledge, useful to the author and opaque to everyone else.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">These problems aren’t unique to Meta. Every organization at a certain scale hits the same wall. The industry has approached it in different ways. Some companies focus on coordinating people better during incidents (Netflix built and open-sourced Dispatch for exactly this), others focus on automating the investigation itself (Meta’s approach), and still others are leaning into AI-driven diagnostics.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">There are at least three distinct layers to incident response:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">Coordination (getting the right people together)</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">Investigation (figuring out what went wrong)</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">Remediation (fixing it).</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Meta invested deepest in the investigation layer, and their approach is worth studying because it has been in production for over five years at a massive scale.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">You can also think about this as a maturity progression from tribal knowledge to wiki runbooks to ad-hoc scripts to testable analyzers to a composable platform. Most teams are stuck somewhere around step two or three, whereas DrP represents step five.</p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro The output is structured findings (both human-readable and machine-readable) and not just a wiki page that someone might skim.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: justify">Analyzers go through code review. They have automated backtesting integrated into the review process, so you can verify an analyzer would have caught last month’s incidents before you deploy it. They ship through a CI/CD process. When the underlying system changes, the analyzer gets updated through the same development workflow as any other code.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">See the diagram below that shows the authoring workflow for the same:</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px SDK also provides shared libraries for common investigation patterns, such as anomaly detection (spotting unusual behavior in metrics), time series correlation (checking whether a metric spike lines up with a deploy or config change), and dimension analysis (automatically slicing metrics by region, device type, or other attributes to isolate where a problem is concentrated). Engineers don’t reinvent these from scratch for each analyzer.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The mental shift matters as much as the technology. DrP has users (on-call engineers), a platform team, deployment pipelines, and usage metrics. It is maintained and improved continuously, not abandoned after the initial author moves teams.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;text-align: justify">Where the Platform Beats the Script</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Writing analyzers as code is the foundation. But the real leverage comes from what happens when you connect them.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">In a microservices architecture, the root cause is rarely in the service showing symptoms. Your API error rate spiked, but the actual cause may be a config change in a storage service three layers down. With standalone scripts, each team can only investigate its own domain. With DrP, analyzers chain across service boundaries. The API analyzer discovers the issue is downstream, invokes the Storage Service analyzer, passes along the context it has already gathered, and gets back a confirmed root cause. This happens automatically, without anyone pinging a Slack channel.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">DrP also integrates directly into the alert lifecycle. Analyzers trigger automatically when an alert fires. Results annotate the alert itself, so the on-call engineer sees the diagnosis alongside the page, before they have opened a single dashboard.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">After the investigation, a post-processing system can close the loop: create a revert task, file a bug, or trigger a mitigation step. And there’s a broader feedback loop too.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">DrP Insights periodically analyzes outputs across all investigations to identify and rank the most common alert causes across the organization. Individual investigations become organizational learning.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;text-align: justify">An Investigation: Start to Finish</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">To make this concrete, here’s what a DrP-powered investigation looks like in practice. This is a possible scenario based on DrP’s documented capabilities, not a specific Meta incident.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Let’s consider that the error rates spike on an API service. The alert fires and auto-triggers the relevant analyzer. From there, the investigation unfolds in a series of automated steps:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">The analyzer pulls error rate data and runs dimension analysis, slicing by region, device type, and data center. It isolates the problem to one region.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">It runs time series correlation, comparing the error spike against other signals like latency, deploy events, and config changes. It finds a strong match with a recent config change on a downstream storage service.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">Since the storage service is a separate dependency, the analyzer chains into the Storage Service analyzer, passing along the regional context. That analyzer confirms the config change pushed response latency past the API’s timeout threshold.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">The findings surface to the on-call engineer as a structured summary: affected region, root cause, correlated timestamp, and a link to the offending change.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">The post-processing system creates a revert task assigned to the storage team.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">The engineer reviews the analysis, approves the revert, and the incident is resolved. The investigation that might have taken 45 minutes of manual work across multiple tools and teams happened in the background before the engineer finished reading the alert.</p></li></ul><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;text-align: justify">Conclusion</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">DrP has reduced mean time to resolve incidents by 20-80% across Meta’s teams, with over 2,000 analyzers in production. Those numbers are compelling, but the lasting takeaway isn’t about a specific tool at a specific company.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Investigation knowledge is too valuable to live in people’s heads or in documents that go stale. It can be codified into testable, composable software.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">However, this doesn’t eliminate the need for human judgment. DrP deliberately keeps engineers in the loop, presenting findings for review rather than auto-remediating. And it’s not free; analyzers are code, and code needs maintenance. You’re trading unpredictable on-call toil for more manageable engineering work. But wherever you work, the question is worth asking: is your team’s debugging knowledge engineered into your system, or is it waiting to walk out the door?</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: Essential Reading For Engineering Leaders  ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌

March 31st, 2026   |   Read online

Tuesday 31st March issue is presented by WorkOS

WorkOS FGA: The Authorization Layer For AI Agents

Every AI agent demo looks magical, but most hit a wall in enterprise deployment. It's not model quality or latency. It's authorization. Authentication proves an agent's identity. Authorization defines its blast radius.

The winners in enterprise AI won't have the most features.They'll be the ones enterprises can safely trust. Learn how WorkOS FGA scopes that blast radius with resource-level permissions.

Read The Deep Dive →

 

How Do You Know If You’re A Good Leader?

— Mike Fisher

tl;dr: “Feeling unsure may not be a sign that you’re failing as a leader. It may be a sign that you’re taking the role seriously enough to do the hardest work first, the work inside your own head. That kind of introspection raises a harder question for the rest of us: How do you actually know if you’re a good leader?”

Leadership Management
 

Nobody Is Coming To Save Your Career

— Steve Huynh

tl;dr: “Most people assume someone will tap them on the shoulder when it’s time. In my experience, that assumption is the single biggest reason high performers get stuck. Here are three truths about who owns your career, and what to do if you realize that you’re trapped on the wrong side of them.”

CareerAdvice
 

WorkOS Pipes: The Connectivity Layer For AI Agents

— Zack Proser, Dan Doorman, Michael Hadley

tl;dr: Your product can't see what's in Slack, GitHub, or Salesforce. Most tools are locked to their own database, blind to everything users actually live in - and that's the ceiling on what you can build. WorkOS Pipes removes it. One API call connects your product to the apps your users already use, so you can pull context across silos, power agents that act across services, and never think about credential management again.

Promoted by WorkOS

Agents
 

What About Juniors?

— Marc Brooker

tl;dr: “In any time of change, the people who can learn and adapt fastest are most likely to succeed. The senior’s advantage is that they have a lot of knowledge and context. The junior’s advantage is that they come in knowing that they need to learn, adapt, and change.”

CareerAdvice

“Anyone can hold the helm when the sea is calm.“

 
— Publilius Syrus

Software Engineering Splits In Three

— Matteo Collina

tl;dr: AI-assisted development shifts software engineering’s bottleneck from coding to judgment, changing how organizations build software. The article outlines three emerging tiers — from tech giants to small businesses — and explains evolving roles, talent needs, and why platforms, guardrails, and senior expertise become critical.

Leadership Management
 

Analyze Privileged Sessions At Scale

tl;dr: Reviewing sessions manually doesn't scale. Teleport analyzes activity across infrastructure, generating summaries, flagging anomalies, and adding context so teams can investigate faster. From audits to incident response, get clear visibility into what actually happened. Investigate sessions faster.

Promoted by Teleport

Observability Incidents
 

Scaling A Monolith To 1M LOC: 113 Pragmatic Lessons From Tech Lead To CTO

— Jack Kinsella

tl;dr: A practical guide to scaling a large codebase, covering performance, system design, monitoring, and team practices. It outlines common issues like database bottlenecks and deployment risks, along with strategies for debugging, testing, and maintaining reliability as systems and teams grow.

Architecture BestPractices
 

Harness Design For Long-Running Application Development

— Prithvi Rajasekaran

tl;dr: “Harness design is key to performance at the frontier of agentic coding. Here's how we pushed Claude further in frontend design and long-running autonomous software engineering.”

Design
 

How To Do AI-Assisted Engineering

— Gregor Ojstersek

tl;dr: Engineers and engineering leaders share how they are doing AI-assisted engineering. They come from a variety of backgrounds and a range of company sizes, from startups to mid-sized and large organizations.

BestPractices
 

Most Popular From Last Issue

How Can Engineering Leaders Assess Their AI Maturity? - Lizzie Matusov

 

Notable Links

Claude Code: Best practice.

Cq: Open standard for shared agent learning.

Nanobrew: The fastest macOS package manager.

Pgmicro: In-process reimplementation of PostgreSQL.

VibeVoice: OS frontier voice AI.

rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Translating between 16 languages means supporting 256 possible pairs, such as Korean to English, French to Thai, Portuguese to Japanese, and so on. One solution is to build a separate model for each pair. However, Roblox decided to build just one.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Roblox is a global platform where more than 70 million people play, create, and socialize every day across more than 15 million active experiences. Users span 180 countries and communicate constantly through in-experience text chat. And a single unified model now handles real-time chat translation across all of those users, at roughly 100 milliseconds per translation and over 5,000 chats per second.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">However, Roblox’s real engineering challenge wasn’t building a model that could translate. It was building a system that could translate at the speed of a conversation without breaking the user experience. In this article, we will look at what Roblox built and the trade-offs they made.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><em>Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from the Roblox Engineering Team. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.</em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;text-align: justify">One Model Versus Many</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Building a separate model for every language pair is the obvious starting point. One model for English to Korean, another for Korean to French, another for French to Thai, and so on.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">With 16 languages, that’s 16 times 16, or 256 individual models. Each one needs its own training data, its own infrastructure, its own maintenance. And when Roblox adds a 17th language, they don’t need a new model. They need 32. The approach grows quadratically, and it collapses under its own weight long before you reach production.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Roblox went a different direction.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">They built a single, unified transformer-based translation model that handles all 256 language directions. The key to making this work is an architecture called Mixture of Experts, or MoE. Instead of every translation request passing through every parameter in the model, a routing mechanism activates only a subset of specialized “expert” subnetworks depending on the input.</p><div justify">Different experts specialize in groups of similar languages. Given a source sentence and a target language, the system activates the relevant expert (or combination of experts) to generate the translation. Think of it as a team of specialist translators sitting behind a single reception desk. A request comes in, the routing layer sends it to the right specialist, and only that specialist does the work. The full team has broad expertise, but any single translation only activates a fraction of it.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">This unified approach creates some great benefits. When all languages are trained together, similar languages actually help each other. For example, Spanish and Portuguese share enough structure that training them in the same model improves translation quality for both. The model also learns enough about each language’s patterns that it can auto-detect the source language, even when the language setting is wrong or missing. It can even handle mixed-language input, where someone types in two languages within the same message, and still produce a reasonable translation into the target language.</p><div The architectural problem was solved, but the serving problem was just getting started.</p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background:
